# Packages

```{r}
library(fpp3)
```

# Hand calculations (match the slides)

## Design matrix and fitted values

Two years of quarterly data, trend $t=1,\dots,8$, seasonal dummies $D_2,D_3,D_4$ (Q1 baseline).
Given coefficients (not estimated): $\beta_0=10,\ \beta_1=0.5,\ \beta_2=-2,\ \beta_3=-3,\ \beta_4=4$.

```{r}
quarters <- rep(1:4, times = 2)
toy <- tibble::tibble(
  t = 1:8,
  Quarter = quarters,
  D2 = as.numeric(quarters == 2),
  D3 = as.numeric(quarters == 3),
  D4 = as.numeric(quarters == 4)
)

beta <- c(Intercept = 10, t = 0.5, D2 = -2, D3 = -3, D4 = 4)

X <- as.matrix(cbind(Intercept = 1, toy[, c("t", "D2", "D3", "D4")]))
toy$fitted <- as.numeric(X %*% beta)
toy
```

You should get fitted values `10.5, 9, 8.5, 16, 12.5, 11, 10.5, 18` — matching the slide table exactly.
Check the trend-only step: $\hat y_8-\hat y_4 = 4\beta_1 = 2$.

# Data: Australian beer production

```{r}
beer <- aus_production |>
  filter(!is.na(Beer)) |>
  select(Quarter, Beer)

beer |> autoplot(Beer) +
  labs(title = "Australian beer production", y = "megalitres")
```

# Fit TSLM (trend + season) on the full series

```{r}
fit <- beer |>
  model(
    snaive = SNAIVE(Beer),
    tslm = TSLM(Beer ~ trend() + season()),
    ets = ETS(Beer)
  )

report(fit |> select(tslm))
# AICc is only comparable within a model class (not TSLM vs ETS vs SNAIVE)
glance(fit |> select(tslm)) |> select(r_squared, adj_r_squared, AICc)
```

```{r}
# Posit Cloud: feasts::ACF() stops if fable innovations come back empty.
e <- lm_resid(
  Beer ~ seq_along(Beer) + factor(quarter(Quarter)),
  beer,
  fit[["tslm"]][[1]]
)
plot_innovations(beer$Quarter, e, "TSLM — innovation residuals")
```

```{r}
fit |> forecast(h = "2 years") |> autoplot(beer, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "TSLM vs ETS vs SNAIVE")
```

# Hold-out evaluation: train through 2007 Q4, test from 2008 Q1

```{r}
train <- beer |> filter_index(. ~ "2007 Q4")
test <- beer |> filter_index("2008 Q1" ~ .)

fit_ho <- train |>
  model(
    snaive = SNAIVE(Beer),
    tslm = TSLM(Beer ~ trend() + season()),
    ets = ETS(Beer)
  )

fc_ho <- fit_ho |> forecast(h = nrow(test))
accuracy(fc_ho, beer) |> arrange(RMSE)
fc_ho |> autoplot(beer, level = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Hold-out forecasts (train through 2007 Q4)")
```

# Is TSLM the problem? Same formula, different training window

FPP3 §7.4 fits the Beer TSLM from 1992 onward. Compare that with the full-sample fit and a
piecewise trend (FPP3 §7.7), on the same hold-out.

```{r}
train92 <- beer |> filter_index("1992 Q1" ~ "2007 Q4")

fit_win <- bind_cols(
  train |> model(
    tslm_1956 = TSLM(Beer ~ trend() + season()),
    tslm_knots = TSLM(Beer ~ trend(knots = yearquarter(c("1975 Q1", "1990 Q1"))) + season()),
    ets = ETS(Beer)
  ),
  train92 |> model(tslm_1992 = TSLM(Beer ~ trend() + season()))
)

fc_win <- fit_win |> forecast(h = nrow(test))
accuracy(fc_win, beer) |> select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |> arrange(RMSE)
```

Now look at the **prediction intervals** (80% and 95%), not just the point forecasts:

```{r}
fc_win |>
  filter(.model %in% c("tslm_1956", "tslm_1992")) |>
  autoplot(beer |> filter_index("1985 Q1" ~ .)) +
  facet_wrap(~.model, ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Same TSLM formula, different training window", y = "Megalitres")
```

The 1956 model has wide intervals, yet the actual values sit near the lower edge: the error is
systematic, not random. Intervals are only trustworthy when the residuals look like white noise.

# Correlation is not causation

Two series with no causal link, both trending upward over 1970--2011.

```{r}
spur <- aus_airpassengers |>
  filter_index("1970" ~ "2011") |>
  left_join(guinea_rice, by = "Year")

fit_spur <- spur |> model(TSLM(Passengers ~ Production))
report(fit_spur)
augment(fit_spur) |> features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 10)
```

A very high $R^2$ and a huge $t$-value, but strongly autocorrelated residuals (small Ljung--Box $p$-value):
the shared trend, not rice, "explains" Australian air travel. We formalise this in Session 10.

# Your turn

1. Add only `trend()` (no season) and compare residual seasonality with `plot_innovations()` (same helper as above). `gg_tsresiduals()` fails on Posit Cloud when the innovation series is empty.
2. Interpret the largest seasonal coefficient (`report()`) in one sentence, relative to the omitted quarter.
3. From the hold-out table above, which model wins on RMSE? The full-sample TSLM has a respectable in-sample $R^2$ --- why does that not protect it on the hold-out?
4. Plot `spur` with `autoplot()` for each series. In one sentence, explain why the regression above is not evidence that rice production causes air travel.
5. Check the residuals of `tslm_1992` with `plot_innovations()` (or a Ljung--Box test). Are they closer to white noise than those of `tslm_1956`? What does that say about trusting each model's prediction intervals?
